clue.text: In his estimation there are no good-byes, only bad ones

definitions.text: In his estimation there are no good-byes, only bad ones

parts.words: In his estimation there are no good-byes, only bad ones
parts.note: in cricket, byes are runs conceded when the ball passes the batsman and the man behind the stumps alike, so for him every bye is a bad one

explanation.surface: A gloomy fellow who never enjoys a farewell, only regrets each parting.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'good-byes' disguises cricket's byes: extras scored when the ball beats the batsman and the gloveman behind the stumps, a black mark against the latter.
explanation.definitionFit: The cricketer stationed behind the stumps is blamed for every bye conceded, so no bye is ever good in his view.

clue.text: Deduce a negative

parts.note: to deduce is to infer
no is a negative reply

explanation.surface: An instruction to reason one's way to a refusal.
explanation.walkthrough: An old-style clue with no separate definition: the whole clue builds the word, Dante's name for hell.
explanation.definitionFit: The two pieces run together into the Italian poet's word for the infernal fiery region.

clue.text: "These foolish things remind me of you "

definitions.text: "These foolish things remind me of you "

parts.words: "These foolish things remind me of you "
parts.note: the 1936 popular song lists trinkets and souvenirs that bring back a lost love

explanation.surface: A line from the popular song about trifles that recall an absent lover.
explanation.definitionFit: Mementos kept for remembrance of someone are exactly the foolish things the song describes.

clue.text: Cigarettes are sold in them

parts.note: cigarettes were commonly sold in packets of twenty, so the clue reads like a sales fact

explanation.surface: A plain statement about how tobacconists package their wares.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Them' suggests shops or kiosks, but it means packets counted by number of smokes.
explanation.definitionFit: Packs of a score of cigarettes are called by that number in the plural.

clue.text: Mrs. Bennet's bugbear

parts.note: in Pride and Prejudice the Longbourn estate is settled on the male heir Mr Collins, to Mrs Bennet's endless complaint

explanation.surface: A literary allusion to what most annoyed Mrs Bennet in Jane Austen's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Bennet is the mother in Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice; the family estate must pass to a male cousin, leaving her five daughters unprovided for.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal settlement restricting inheritance to male heirs is what keeps Longbourn from the Bennet daughters.

clue.text: That's true enough

parts.note: true in the builder's sense of exactly vertical, as tested with a weighted line

explanation.surface: A grudging concession in an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'True' looks like agreement, but it is the builder's word for perfectly upright.
explanation.definitionFit: Something exactly vertical is described by the word for the lead weight on a builder's line.

clue.text: Vulgarian's vague description of a narrow racecourse victory

parts.note: a rough estimate is a vague one

parts.words: description of a narrow racecourse victory
parts.note: a horse that wins by a neck wins by a narrow margin

explanation.surface: A boorish punter's imprecise account of a close finish at the races.
explanation.definitionFit: A coarse, uncultivated person is a synonym for a rowdy tough.

clue.text: No man of business

parts.note: a person with no business at all, one who does nothing, rather than a non-commercial person

explanation.surface: A dismissive description of someone unfit for commerce.
explanation.definitionFit: A loafer who does no work at all is the opposite of a busy man.

clue.text: Caught his clear accents, Made him our to live and to die" (Browning)

definitions.text: Caught his clear accents, Made him our to live and to die" (Browning)

parts.words: Caught his clear accents, Made him our to live and to die" (Browning)
parts.note: a gap-fill from Browning's poem The Lost Leader

explanation.surface: A quotation from Robert Browning with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing word comes from Browning's The Lost Leader, about followers who took a leader as their model.
explanation.definitionFit: The followers took the leader as their model or example, the word missing from the line.

clue.text: Ten if Fred were changed

indicators.note: the letters of the three words are altered in order to form a new word

explanation.surface: A puzzling remark about what would happen if a man named Fred were altered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'were changed' shuffles TENIFFRED, and the result itself means changed, so the whole clue is both wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something changed is altered, no longer the same as before.

clue.text: It moves with the swallows

parts.note: swallows are gulps in the throat, not migrating birds; the fleshy flap at the back of the mouth moves with each one

explanation.surface: Something that migrates along with the birds each season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swallows' suggests birds; it is acts of swallowing.
explanation.definitionFit: The small fleshy lobe hanging at the back of the soft palate rises during each gulp.

clue.text: They are found in pearls but not oysters

definitions.text: They are found in pearls but not oysters

indicators.note: says the wanted letters sit inside the word that follows, not in real shellfish

explanation.surface: A natural-history riddle about where certain things turn up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'are found in' points inside 'pearls'; the whole clue also describes noblemen whose coronets are set with pearls, while oysters have none of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Noblemen of this rank wear coronets ornamented with pearls, so they are found among pearls.

clue.text: A du Maurier "creation "

parts.note: George du Maurier's novel Trilby gave its name to the soft felt hat worn in the stage version

explanation.surface: A reference to something devised by the novelist George du Maurier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creation' in quotes hints at millinery: the hat took its name from du Maurier's 1894 novel Trilby.
explanation.definitionFit: The soft felt hat with an indented crown is named after the heroine of du Maurier's novel.

clue.text: The volume lacks volume

parts.note: the first volume is a book, the second is bulk: a slim little book

explanation.surface: A paradoxical remark about a book with little substance.
explanation.definitionFit: A small thin pamphlet is a book without much bulk.

clue.text: Brief, brave and glorious was his young 9 (Byron)

definitions.text: Brief, brave and glorious was his young 9 (Byron)

parts.words: Brief, brave and glorious was his young 9 (Byron)
parts.note: a gap-fill from Byron's Childe Harold, on the short life of the soldier Marceau

explanation.surface: A quotation from Lord Byron with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The number stands where the missing word goes in Byron's line about the young general Marceau.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's course through life, especially a professional one, is the missing word.

clue.text: Short deal (anag.)

indicators.note: the bracketed abbreviation openly tells the solver to rearrange the preceding words

explanation.surface: A bare instruction to rearrange two words.
explanation.walkthrough: An old-style clue with no definition: only the rearrangement gives the answer, a Hampshire town that is home of the British Army.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hampshire garrison town is the only sensible arrangement of the letters.

clue.text: They might be fringes, and are for hands

definitions.text: They might be fringes, and are for hands

indicators.note: signals that the letters of the word could be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: A remark about decorative edging and what hands are made of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might be' signals the shuffle of FRINGES; the rest says what the result is: digits belonging to hands.
explanation.definitionFit: The digits of the hand are what the rearranged word names.

clue.text: The fanatic Daniel told to go dancing

parts.note: a fan is short for fanatic

explanation.surface: A zealot named Daniel is instructed to go off and dance.
explanation.definitionFit: A lively Spanish dance, so the word stands for the activity of dancing itself.

clue.text: A verb in the imperative mood, it seems

definitions.text: A verb in the imperative mood, it seems

parts.words: A verb in the imperative mood, it seems
parts.note: the imperative mood is a grammar term, but read as a temper it means a demanding frame of mind

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson about verbs that give commands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Imperative mood' is the grammatical form for commands, but here it means a peremptory frame of mind.
explanation.definitionFit: To demand something forcefully is a verb whose very meaning is being imperative.

clue.text: and Jorkins

parts.note: Dickens's law firm in David Copperfield is named for two partners; the second is Jorkins, and the first is the missing name

explanation.surface: Half of a firm's name, as if completing a brass plate.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's David Copperfield, the proctors' firm Spenlow and Jorkins employs David; the missing first partner is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The senior partner whose name precedes Jorkins on the firm's title in the Dickens novel.

clue.text: Painter who took a vehicle to the bank

parts.note: a van is a vehicle
a dyke is an embankment

explanation.surface: An artist who drove a van down to the riverbank, or to his bank.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony van Dyck, the Flemish portrait painter, is spelt Vandyke in English usage.
explanation.definitionFit: The Flemish portraitist of Charles I's court, anglicised in spelling.

clue.text: Smart

parts.note: smart in the sense of neatly and stylishly dressed

explanation.definitionFit: Neatly turned out in appearance is a synonym for spruce or trim.

clue.text: The servant begins where the master ends

definitions.text: The servant begins where the master ends

indicators.note: only the closing part of the word master is kept

parts.note: the word master itself

indicators.note: only the opening part of the word servant is kept

parts.note: the word servant itself

explanation.surface: A maxim about where a servant's duties take up from his employer's.
explanation.walkthrough: An old-style clue without a separate definition: 'ends' keeps TER from master, 'begins' keeps SE from servant, and the servant's piece comes where the master's stops.
explanation.definitionFit: The joined pieces make the word for brief and curt in speech, fitting for a master's orders.

clue.text: Is it populated by the uninitiated'?

definitions.text: Is it populated by the uninitiated'?

parts.words: Is it populated by the uninitiated'?
parts.note: the uninitiated are green, so a country full of them would be a land of the green

explanation.surface: A sly question about a place full of novices.
explanation.walkthrough: Green means inexperienced, so the Arctic island's name is read as a land of greenhorns.
explanation.definitionFit: The great Arctic island's name can be read as a country of novices.

clue.text: Scots darkness is not in Germany

definitions.meaning: in Scots, the word for night

explanation.surface: A claim that Scottish gloom is absent from Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scots spelling of night coincides with the German word meaning not.

clue.text: The cur turns tail and he follows

definitions.text: The cur turns tail and he follows

indicators.note: the word he comes after the turned dog
a dog turning tail swings round, so the word cur is read backwards

explanation.surface: A cowardly dog runs off, with its owner close behind.
explanation.walkthrough: An old-style clue without a separate definition: 'turns tail' makes RUC. A ruche is a gathered frill on a dress.
explanation.definitionFit: The pieces make the dressmaker's word for a pleated or gathered strip of fabric.

clue.text: It's small in India

parts.note: the Hindi-derived Anglo-Indian word for small or junior

explanation.surface: A remark that something is little in India.
explanation.walkthrough: Anglo-Indian usage, as in chota peg, a small drink.
explanation.definitionFit: The Anglo-Indian adjective meaning little or younger, borrowed from Hindi.

clue.text: It's left

parts.note: left in the sense of left behind, surviving from the past, rather than a direction

explanation.definitionFit: A surviving object from an earlier age is something remaining after the rest has gone.

clue.text: One's confused with a punch

indicators.note: with places the shuffled letters alongside, after the punch

parts.note: taken as the tool or blow, the word itself

indicators.note: the letters of the word are muddled into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone mistaken for a blow, or for the drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confused' makes EONS from 'One's'. A puncheon is a large cask, and also a punching tool, hence the confusion with a punch.
explanation.definitionFit: One meaning is a stamping tool used for punching, so it is easily mistaken for one.

clue.text: This small creature provides the three desiderata for navigation

definitions.text: This small creature provides the three desiderata for navigation

parts.words: This small creature provides the three desiderata for navigation
parts.note: to sail you need water, a boat and a man to crew it; the insect's name supplies all three

explanation.surface: A tiny animal that supplies everything a sailor needs.
explanation.walkthrough: The aquatic bug's name splits into WATER, BOAT and MAN, everything needed to navigate.
explanation.definitionFit: An aquatic insect that rows itself along with oar-like legs.
